intervals.label: construction
intervals.locator: abstract (arXiv:1808.07445); Simons Foundation press release of 3 June 2024
intervals.note: Start is a lower bound: the August 2018 science-goals paper says SO is "being built"; no source states when construction began. End: the 2024 press release says the "completion of the observatory's main construction phase coincided with Simons' 86th birthday on April 25"; the year (2024) is inferred from the release date (3 June 2024) and Jim Simons's death on 10 May 2024, which the release dates "a few weeks later".
intervals.quote: The Simons Observatory (SO) is a new cosmic microwave background experiment being built on Cerro Toco in Chile, due to begin observations in the early 2020s.

intervals.label: science observations
intervals.locator: Simons Foundation press release of 3 June 2024, paragraph 1
intervals.note: Start is the press-release date: the release says the observatory "just completed its main construction phase" and observers "have begun searching"; earlier engineering or first-light observations (the SATs) are not sourced here. Status as of 26 October 2026: the Simons Foundation release of 22 October 2026 says "the Simons Observatory in Chile is completely online and conducting science operations".
intervals.quote: From a vantage point high in the Chilean Andes, cosmologists with the Simons Observatory have begun searching for evidence of what happened in the minuscule fraction of a second that followed the Big Bang.

intervals.label: Large Aperture Telescope first light
intervals.locator: Simons Foundation press release of 17 March 2025
intervals.note: First celestial image (Mars) of the six-metre LAT, after mirror installation in February 2025.
intervals.quote: The Simons Observatory’s Large Aperture Telescope captured this first light image of Mars on February 22, 2025.

placements.quote: Located at an elevation of 5190 meters on Cerro Toco in the Atacama Desert of Northern Chile, an hour from the town of San Pedro de Atacama

diameter.quote: SO currently consists of three 0.5 meter diameter Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs), and one six-meter diameter Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

sensor_count.quote: the new observatory incorporates more than 16 times as many detectors — 98,000 in total.

telescope_count.note: Sum of the quote's three Small Aperture Telescopes and one Large Aperture Telescope (3 + 1 = 4). The page says "currently" and adds that further Small Aperture Telescopes are planned (SO:UK, SO:JP), which are not counted.
telescope_count.quote: SO currently consists of three 0.5 meter diameter Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs), and one six-meter diameter Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).

summary.plain: One six-metre telescope and three half-metre telescopes on a Chilean mountain, carrying about 98,000 detectors that map the Big Bang afterglow far more deeply than earlier ground-based instruments.
summary.technical: Large Aperture Telescope (6 m crossed Dragone) plus three 0.5 m Small Aperture Telescopes at 5190 m on Cerro Toco; six bands 27-280 GHz; three more SATs (SO:UK, SO:JP) to be added.

technology.quote: SO currently consists of three 0.5 meter diameter Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs), and one six-meter diameter Large Aperture Telescope (LAT).
technology.value: One 6 m Large Aperture Telescope and three 0.5 m Small Aperture Telescopes with transition-edge-sensor bolometer cameras in six frequency bands.
